The post 9 Best AI Gateways in 2026: Bifrost, Portkey, LiteLLM, Kong and 5 More Ranked appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> An AI gateway is a control layer between your application and model providers. It gives every service one API for many models. It also centralizes routing, retries, failover, caching, budgets and logs. This guide presents the best AI gateways for production teams in 2026. The market moved fast this year. Palo Alto Networks closed its acquisition of Portkey on May 29. Mintlify acquired Helicone , which now runs in maintenance mode. LiteLLM survived a PyPI supply chain compromise in March. Your gateway choice now carries vendor and security risk, not just feature risk. TL;DR Best overall for self-hosted performance: Bifrost. Go binary, Apache 2.0, 11 µs published overhead at 5,000 RPS. Best open-source gateway with guardrails: Portkey. MIT license, 1,600+ models, now backed by Palo Alto Networks. Widest adoption: LiteLLM. 53.8K GitHub stars, 100+ providers, Python-first. Best for API platform teams: Kong AI Gateway. LLM, MCP and A2A traffic in one stack. Best managed options: Cloudflare (edge, free core), Vercel (zero markup), OpenRouter (model access). How We Ranked These AI Gateways We weighted 6 criteria for production use: Performance evidence: published overhead, and how it was measured. The post Datalab Releases OmniParseBench: An Open OCR Benchmark With 16,288 Pass/Fail Tests to Audit OCR Parsers appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Datalab has released OmniParseBench , an open OCR benchmark for document parsers. It scores parsers with 16,288 yes/no tests on 2,937 pages from 2,343 documents. The pages span 92 languages. The dataset and code are public. It helps engineers answer a sharper question than a leaderboard does: which parser handles documents like mine? Datalab sells a parser, and its own top setting, Datalab accurate, ranks second on the launch leaderboard, behind Gemini 3.8 Flash. Is it deployable? Yes. OmniParseBench is an evaluation harness, not a model. It installs with uv pip install omni-parse-bench, needs Python 3.11+, and scores outputs offline with no API keys. TL;DR Size: 16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 documents, 22 suites, 92 languages. Runs on: any machine with Python 3.11+. Scoring needs no network. Vendor runs need each vendor’s API key. Performance: the top 3 reported systems sit within 1.3 headline points. Best: Gemini 3.8 Flash leads at 92.9; Datalab accurate follows at 92.7.* Bottom line: every score is a share of pass/fail tests, sliceable by tag. * used in building some tests What is OmniParseBench? OmniParseBench is a document-parsing benchmark from Datalab where every test is a yes/no question about 1 page. A parser’s score is the share of tests it passes. Datalab built it to be clear, auditable and explorable. Why build another OCR benchmark? Datalab names two problems with existing benchmarks. olmOCR-bench showed that pass/fail unit tests work. Datalab now calls it saturated. In its view, top systems are separated by output conventions and overfitting, not reading. Each olmOCR-bench test also sits in 1 bucket, set by its page’s source. A handwritten table gets averaged into whichever bucket its page landed in. ParseBench from LlamaIndex splits parsing into 5 capabilities, each with its own metric. Datalab argues those scores share no unit, so they cannot be compared or combined cleanly. How does OmniParseBench scoring work? The final score is the mean of 3 family scores: text, tables and layout. Five test types feed those families: present: a text, number or equation appears (text) order: text A comes before text B (text) repeat: a line appears exactly N times (text) table_cell: a cell sits under given headings and beside given neighbors (tables) layout_kind: the block holding a line is a heading, text or table (layout) Numbers must match digit for digit, though 1,240 matches 1240. Equations are compared by what KaTeX renders, so \frac{a}{b} equals \dfrac{a}{b}. Each decision is pass, fail, unsupported or error. The last 2 are left out of every score. No model judges the outputs; the scorer is open code . What do tags and derivations add? A test checks one or more args, each of which is the content at one place on the page. Each arg carries tags on 5 axes: structure, rendering, role, script and language. Scripts use ISO 15924 codes; languages use ISO 639-3 codes. Tags never decide a verdict or the headline. They only select tests, so any slice gets its own score. The table tag covers 6,767 tests on 1,000 pages from 875 documents. English covers 10,089 tests. Non-English languages cover 1,931 tests on 529 pages from 321 documents. Every test also records its derivation, meaning how its answer was established. There are 10 derivations . They include publisher JATS XML, the PDF text layer, authored pages, olmOCR-bench tests, model panels and human review. What are the OmniParseBench launch results? Claude Sonnet 5.5 posts the top text (93.1) and tables (95.4) scores. Its layout score of 77.5 pulls its headline to 88.7. Reducto leads layout at 95.8. Datalab also plotted each headline against median latency and price per 1,000 pages. Latency was measured on 200 sampled pages, sent 8 at a time. Datalab does not top its own benchmark. It scores parsers with 16,288 yes/no tests on 2,937 pages from 2,343 documents. The pages span 92 languages. The dataset and code are public. It helps engineers answer a sharper question than a leaderboard does: which parser handles documents like mine? Datalab sells a parser, and its own top setting, Datalab accurate, ranks second on the launch leaderboard, behind Gemini 3.8 Flash. Is it deployable? Yes. OmniParseBench is an evaluation harness, not a model. It installs with uv pip install omni-parse-bench, needs Python 3.11+, and scores outputs offline with no API keys. TL;DR Size: 16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 documents, 22 suites, 92 languages. Runs on: any machine with Python 3.11+. Scoring needs no network. Vendor runs need each vendor’s API key. Performance: the top 3 reported systems sit within 1.3 headline points. Best: Gemini 3.8 Flash leads at 92.9; Datalab accurate follows at 92.7.* Bottom line: every score is a share of pass/fail tests, sliceable by tag. * used in building some tests What is OmniParseBench? OmniParseBench is a document-parsing benchmark from Datalab where every test is a yes/no question about 1 page. A parser’s score is the share of tests it passes. Datalab built it to be clear, auditable and explorable. Why build another OCR benchmark? Datalab names two problems with existing benchmarks. olmOCR-bench showed that pass/fail unit tests work. Datalab now calls it saturated. In its view, top systems are separated by output conventions and overfitting, not reading. Each olmOCR-bench test also sits in 1 bucket, set by its page’s source. A handwritten table gets averaged into whichever bucket its page landed in. ParseBench from LlamaIndex splits parsing into 5 capabilities, each with its own metric. Datalab argues those scores share no unit, so they cannot be compared or combined cleanly. How does OmniParseBench scoring work? The final score is the mean of 3 family scores: text, tables and layout. Five test types feed those families: present: a text, number or equation appears (text) order: text A comes before text B (text) repeat: a line appears exactly N times (text) table_cell: a cell sits under given headings and beside given neighbors (tables) layout_kind: the block holding a line is a heading, text or table (layout) Numbers must match digit for digit, though 1,240 matches 1240. Equations are compared by what KaTeX renders, so \frac{a}{b} equals \dfrac{a}{b}. Each decision is pass, fail, unsupported or error. The last 2 are left out of every score. No model judges the outputs; the scorer is open code . What do tags and derivations add? A test checks one or more args, each of which is the content at one place on the page. Each arg carries tags on 5 axes: structure, rendering, role, script and language. Scripts use ISO 15924 codes; languages use ISO 639-3 codes. Tags never decide a verdict or the headline. They only select tests, so any slice gets its own score. The table tag covers 6,767 tests on 1,000 pages from 875 documents. English covers 10,089 tests. Non-English languages cover 1,931 tests on 529 pages from 321 documents. Every test also records its derivation, meaning how its answer was established. There are 10 derivations . They include publisher JATS XML, the PDF text layer, authored pages, olmOCR-bench tests, model panels and human review. What are the OmniParseBench launch results? Worst: 71.6% on τ-Voice, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. Bottom line: Best: top composite score at 0.81 s time to first audio. Worst: not the leader on agentic task resolution or raw speech reasoning. What is Grok Voice 3.0? Grok Voice 3.0 is SpaceXAI’s flagship realtime voice model, exposed as grok-voice-3.0 on the /v1/realtime WebSocket endpoint . The grok-voice-latest alias already points to it, so existing agents switched automatically. SpaceXAI has not published parameter counts or architecture details. Reasoning is on by default ( reasoning.effort: "high" ) and can be set to "none" for faster turns. Server-side voice activity detection handles barge-in. Tools run inside the session: collections search, web search, X search, remote MCP servers and custom functions. How does Grok Voice 3.0 perform on benchmarks? The AA Speech-to-Speech Index is an equal-weighted average of 4 components. Those are Big Bench Audio reasoning, τ-Voice agentic performance, Speech Agent Arena preference and task success rate. Grok Voice 3.0 scores 86.9. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) scores 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking 82.6. Grok Voice 2.0 scored 81.3. Component results are strong, not uniformly first: Big Bench Audio: 98.5%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 99.7%. Full Duplex Bench: 97.0%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 98.9%. Task success rate: 94.8%, up from 94.6% for Grok Voice 2.0. Speech Agent Arena Elo: 1070, the highest among the 4 models compared here. τ-Voice: 71.6%, up from 56.5%, but below GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. ServiceNow’s EVA-Bench scores enterprise voice agents on accuracy and experience. SpaceXAI reports a top accuracy score of 74%. Is Grok Voice 3.0 fast and cheap? Artificial Analysis measures 0.81 s time to first audio. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) measures 1.34 s, so SpaceXAI’s “40% lower latency” claim checks out. Grok Voice 2.0 was faster, though, at 0.70 s. On cost, SpaceXAI cites Artificial Analysis cost per Big Bench Audio task. Grok Voice 3.0 costs $0.025 per task, versus $0.030 for GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) and $0.055 for GPT-Realtime-2.1 (High). On AA’s cost per hour of input audio, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking is cheaper: $3.50 versus $4.80. List prices are not directly comparable.
